Stances

立ち方8
Video
Musubi dachi結び立ち

informal attention stance

Heels together, toes turned out about 45°, arms relaxed at the sides. This is where you stand to bow in and out of the dojo.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Heikō dachi平行立ち

parallel stance

Feet parallel and about shoulder-width apart, weight even, knees soft. The natural standing position most kata open from.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Sanchin dachi三戦立ち

hourglass stance

Gōjū-ryū's signature stance. One foot half a step forward, both feet turned in, knees drawn together and the whole body under tension while you breathe.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Neko ashi dachi猫足立ち

cat stance

Roughly 90% of the weight sits on the bent back leg. Only the ball of the front foot rests on the floor, so it can kick or slide without a weight shift.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Shiko dachi四股立ち

square stance

A wide, deep stance with the feet turned out 45° and the knees pressed open over them. Hips sink straight down — it builds rooting and hip power.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Zenkutsu dachi前屈立ち

front stance

Long stance with about 70% of the weight on the bent front leg and the back leg driven straight. Used to deliver stepping techniques forward.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Kōkutsu dachi後屈立ち

back stance

The mirror of front stance: weight loads onto the bent rear leg, front leg light and straight. A defensive stance that lets you pull back out of range.

PhotosYouTube
Tsuru ashi dachi鶴足立ち

crane stance

Balanced on one bent leg with the other foot tucked in behind the supporting knee. Appears in Seiyunchin and Kururunfa, usually just before a kick or a drop.

PhotosFind video

Punches

突き6
Video
Choku zuki直突き

straight punch

The basic punch: fist travels straight out from the hip, forearm rotating so the knuckles land palm-down. No step — practised on the spot from a natural stance.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Oi zuki追い突き

lunge punch

Step forward into front stance and punch with the hand on the same side as the leading leg, so the whole body mass travels behind the fist.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Gyaku zuki逆突き

reverse punch

From front stance, the rear hand punches as the hips snap square to the target. Karate's main power punch — the hip rotation, not the arm, supplies the force.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Kizami zuki刻み突き

jab

A fast snapping punch with the lead hand from fighting stance. Used to measure distance, interrupt an attack, or open the way for something heavier.

PhotosYouTube
Mawashi zuki回し突き

roundhouse punch

A hooking punch that swings in a horizontal arc with the elbow lifted, landing on the side of the jaw or ribs rather than straight on.

PhotosFind video
Ura zuki裏突き

close punch

A short punch thrown with the elbow still bent, palm facing up. Made for infighting range, where a full extension would overshoot the target.

PhotosFind video

Strikes

打ち6
Video
Uraken uchi裏拳打ち

backfist strike

The arm folds across the chest, then the fist whips out from the elbow and snaps back, landing with the back of the knuckles on the temple or ribs.

PhotosYouTube
Shutō uchi手刀打ち

knife-hand strike

An open-hand chop with the outer edge of the palm, swung in from beside the ear into the neck or collarbone. The hand stays firm with the thumb tucked.

PhotosFind video
Haitō uchi背刀打ち

ridge-hand strike

The mirror of the knife-hand: the strike sweeps outward and lands on the thumb-side edge of the hand, typically into the neck or the side of the head.

PhotosFind video
Tettsui uchi鉄槌打ち

hammer-fist strike

The bottom of the clenched fist drops like a hammer — straight down onto a collarbone or grabbing arm, or sideways into the ribs. Heavy rather than fast.

PhotosFind video
Empi uchi肘打ち

elbow strike

At close range the elbow becomes the weapon, driven forward, up, back or across. Short travel, very little that can go wrong, and nothing to break.

PhotosFind video
Nukite貫手

spear-hand strike

Fingers held straight and braced together, thrust like a blade into soft targets — the throat, the floating ribs, the solar plexus.

PhotosFind video

Kicks

蹴り7
Video
Mae geri前蹴り

front kick

The knee lifts first, then the lower leg snaps straight out and back again. Contact is with the ball of the foot, toes pulled back out of the way.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Mawashi geri回し蹴り

roundhouse kick

The knee comes up to the side, then the hip rotates over and the leg whips around parallel to the floor. Lands with the instep, ball of the foot, or shin.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Yoko geri横蹴り

side kick

The kick travels sideways with the body leaning away from it, striking with the outer edge of the foot (sokutō) rather than the ball.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Ushiro geri後ろ蹴り

back kick

A kick driven straight out behind you, heel first, with the body folding forward as the leg extends. Usually thrown after turning.

PhotosYouTube
Hiza geri膝蹴り

knee strike

The knee is driven upward into the body at close range, normally while both hands pull the opponent down onto it.

PhotosFind video
Kansetsu geri関節蹴り

joint kick

A low stamping kick into the side or front of the knee joint. Short, blunt and aimed at taking the opponent's base away.

PhotosFind video
Kin geri金蹴り

groin kick

A rising snap kick to the groin using the instep or shin. Short travel, no wind-up, often thrown off the back leg in kihon combinations.

PhotosFind video

Blocks

受け7
Video
Age uke揚げ受け

rising block

The forearm travels up and outward to lift a head-height attack clear, finishing at an angle just above the forehead with the fist past the far temple.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Gedan barai下段払い

downward sweep

The arm sweeps down and across the front of the body to clear a low attack such as a front kick, finishing above the leading thigh.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Soto uke外受け

outside block

The forearm comes from outside the body inward across the centreline, catching a chest-height punch on the outer edge of the arm.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Uchi uke内受け

inside block

The opposite path to soto uke — the forearm starts near the body and drives outward, pushing the attack away from the centreline.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Shutō uke手刀受け

knife-hand block

An open-hand guard: the leading hand blocks with the palm edge while the other stays at the solar plexus. Almost always paired with back stance.

PhotosYouTube
Video
Mawashi uke回し受け

circular block

Gōjū-ryū's own two-handed block, drawn from Sanchin and Tenshō. Both open hands turn through a circle — one high, one low — redirecting rather than meeting force.

PhotosYouTube
Kake uke掛け受け

hooking block

The hand hooks over the incoming arm and pulls it off line, trapping the attacker for a moment so the other hand can strike into the gap.

PhotosFind video

Commands & etiquette

16
礼
Rei礼

bow

The bow. Used entering and leaving the dojo, and to the sensei and partners. Eyes stay up in a martial context.

立礼
Ritsurei立礼

standing bow

Bow performed from standing, normally from musubi dachi.

座礼
Zarei座礼

kneeling bow

Bow performed from seiza, hands placed left then right on the floor.

正座
Seiza正座

formal kneeling

Kneeling posture used at the start and end of class, usually with mokusō.

黙想
Mokusō黙想

silent meditation

A short period of stillness and breathing to settle the mind before or after training.

気を付け
Kiotsuke気を付け

attention

Command to come to attention.

用意
Yōi用意

ready

Command to assume the ready position, normally heikō dachi.

始め
Hajime始め

begin

Command to start.

止め
Yame止め

stop

Command to stop.

回って
Mawatte回って

turn

Command to turn and face the other way, used in moving basics.

直れ
Naore直れ

return

Command to return to the natural position.

先生
Sensei先生

teacher

The instructor. Literally one who has gone before.

先輩
Sempai先輩

senior student

A student senior to you in the dojo.

道場
Dōjō道場

training hall

The place of the way — where training happens.

道着
Dōgi道着

training uniform

The uniform, commonly shortened to gi. Gōjū-ryū gi are traditionally heavier and shorter in the sleeve.

帯
Obi帯

belt

The belt, showing grade. Tied with the knot centred and both ends level.

Levels & directions

12
上段
Jōdan上段

upper level

Head and neck height. A technique named jōdan is aimed there.

中段
Chūdan中段

middle level

Chest and stomach height — the most common target level in kihon.

下段
Gedan下段

lower level

Below the belt: groin, thighs, knees.

左
Hidari左

left

Left side. Hidari sanchin dachi means left foot forward.

右
Migi右

right

Right side.

前
Mae前

front

Forward. As in mae geri, front kick.

後ろ
Ushiro後ろ

rear

Behind. As in ushiro geri, back kick.

横
Yoko横

side

Sideways. As in yoko geri, side kick.

外
Soto外

outside

From outside inward, describing the path of a block or strike.

内
Uchi内

inside

From inside outward. Also means strike when used as uchi waza.

逆
Gyaku逆

reverse

Opposite side to the leading leg, as in gyaku zuki.

諸手
Morote諸手

both hands

Two-handed version of a technique, as in morote uke.

Body weapons

12
正拳
Seiken正拳

forefist

The first two knuckles of a closed fist — the standard punching surface.

Photos
裏拳
Uraken裏拳

backfist

The back of the knuckles, used in whipping strikes.

Photos
鉄槌
Tettsui鉄槌

hammer fist

The muscled bottom edge of the fist.

Photos
手刀
Shutō手刀

knife hand

The outer edge of the open hand, thumb tucked.

Photos
背刀
Haitō背刀

ridge hand

The thumb-side edge of the open hand.

Photos
底掌
Teishō底掌

palm heel

The heel of the palm — a favourite Gōjū-ryū striking surface.

Photos
貫手
Nukite貫手

spear hand

Braced fingertips used against soft targets.

Photos
肘
Hiji / Empi肘

elbow

The elbow, used at close range.

Photos
膝
Hiza膝

knee

The knee, used in clinch range.

Photos
腰
Koshi腰

ball of the foot

The ball of the foot, with toes pulled back. Used in mae geri.

Photos
足刀
Sokutō足刀

foot edge

The outer blade of the foot, used in yoko geri.

Photos
踵

The heel, used in stamping and back kicks.

Concepts

16
剛
Gō剛

hard

The hard half of the style's name: linear, direct, forceful technique.

柔
Jū柔

soft

The soft half of the name: yielding, circular, redirecting technique. Gōjū means hard-soft.

基本
Kihon基本

basics

The fundamental techniques, practised on the spot or moving (ido kihon).

型
Kata型

form

A fixed sequence of techniques that stores the system's knowledge.

分解
Bunkai分解

analysis

Taking a kata apart to work out what the movements are actually for.

組手
Kumite組手

sparring

Partner work, from fixed pre-arranged drills through to free sparring.

気合
Kiai気合

spirit shout

The shout at the moment of commitment, tightening the abdomen and focusing the technique.

決め
Kime決め

focus

The instant of total tension at the end of a technique, then immediate release.

残心
Zanshin残心

remaining mind

Continued awareness after a technique finishes — you have not switched off.

M
Muchimi

heavy sticky movement

A heavy, adhering quality of movement particular to Gōjū-ryū, felt in kake uke and mawashi uke.

C
Chinkuchi

momentary whole-body tension

An Okinawan term for locking the whole body for an instant at the point of impact.

補助運動
Hōjō undō補助運動

supplementary training

Conditioning with traditional tools — chiishi, nigiri game, ishi sashi, makiwara.

丹田
Tanden丹田

centre

The point below the navel treated as the body's centre of power and breathing.

息吹
Ibuki息吹

forceful breathing

The audible tensioned breathing used in Sanchin.

移動
Ido移動

moving

Moving basics — technique performed while stepping, as opposed to on the spot.

体捌き
Tai sabaki体捌き

body shifting

Moving the body off the line of attack rather than meeting it head on.

Kata

12
三戦
Sanchin三戦

three battles

The core kata of the style: slow, tensed, breathing-driven. Everything else is built on it.

Photos
転掌
Tenshō転掌

revolving palms

The soft counterpart to Sanchin, using open-hand circular movement.

Photos
撃砕第一
Gekisai dai ichi撃砕第一

attack and smash 1

The first kata taught, developed by Chōjun Miyagi in the 1940s to introduce basics.

Photos
撃砕第二
Gekisai dai ni撃砕第二

attack and smash 2

Follows Gekisai dai ichi and introduces open-hand technique, neko ashi dachi and muchimi.

Photos
砕破
Saifa砕破

smash and tear

Introduces body evasion, hammer fists and rapid changes of direction.

Photos
制引戦
Seiyunchin制引戦

control and pull

Contains no kicks. Built on shiko dachi and pulling, off-balancing hand work.

Photos
四向戦
Shisōchin四向戦

four directions

Open-hand thrusts and elbow techniques worked in four directions.

Photos
三十六手
Sanseru三十六手

36 hands

Attacks the limbs and joints, with low kicks and close-range entries.

Photos
十八手
Sēpai十八手

18 hands

Advanced kata mixing circular deflection with sudden angular attack.

Photos
久留頓破
Kururunfa久留頓破

holding on long and striking suddenly

Marked by long pauses then explosive bursts, with heavy use of neko ashi dachi.

Photos
十三手
Sēsan十三手

13 hands

Direct, linear kata focused on close-range control and precise angles.

Photos
壱百零八手
Suparinpei壱百零八手

108 hands

The longest and most advanced kata in the system, containing the whole curriculum.
